column4: The section’s dictionary branch for ء خ ر includes a deferred due and fruit kept to the end of harvest; Khidr says the orphans’ treasure is held until they reach full strength, when they can recover it. The retained value is for a later, appointed time.

Yusuf’s plan says to sow for seven years and leave the grain in its ears except a little for eating. This is an explicit crop kept through its growing and harvest stages for a later need, close to the section’s palm fruit remaining until the final picking.
The stored grain is to carry Egypt through seven severe years. It shows what the previous verse’s harvest delay secures: provision held over for the lean period.
After the seven lean years, a year of rain and pressing follows. The later relief completes the sequence of storing provision and receiving its yield afterward.
The verse names date palms and says to give their due on the day of harvest, يوم حصاده. This ties the section’s date-palm branch to an explicitly appointed harvest and its yield.

After the child’s death, God intends a replacement “better” in purity and affection. The section’s خ ي ر branch concerns choosing what is better; this is a painful first loss followed by a promised better outcome.

The fighters ask to be delayed to a near term, then are told that worldly enjoyment is little and the Hereafter is better for the God-fearing. It joins the section’s named delay (ء خ ر) directly to its first/later valuation.

The dying person asks, لولا أخرتني, for a short deferment in which to give charity. The following verse says a soul is not delayed once its appointed term comes; the request makes the section’s deferred-time sense concrete.

If God seized people immediately for wrongdoing, none would remain, but He postpones them to an appointed term; when it arrives, they can neither delay nor advance it. This directly develops delay with a fixed endpoint.
The verse says God defers people until a specified term, after which they cannot delay it. Its postponement and deadline make explicit the appointment implicit in the section’s later gift.

The creditor is told to grant respite to a debtor in hardship until ease. The section’s dictionary branch for ء خ ر gives a sale on credit as waiting for payment; this is the Quran’s concrete case of payment deferred.

The verse begins with a debt contracted for a specified term and orders that it be written down. This supplies a concrete contractual form for the section’s deferred-sale image: payment is due later at an agreed time.

Khidr promises, سأُنَبِّئُكَ بتأويل, that he will explain later what Moses could not bear. The section’s dictionary sense of تأويل is an outcome or where a matter comes to; this verse makes the explanation itself deferred.

The boat is damaged before Khidr explains that a king would otherwise seize every intact boat. What first appears harmful has a protective later outcome, the same before/after pattern the section develops.

Khidr says the child’s death is tied to what the parents would face and to God’s intended replacement, explained in the next verse. The row’s contribution is the painful first event whose later meaning is withheld.
Yusuf calls the family’s arrival and bowing the تأويل of his earlier dream, which God has made true. This is the section’s lexical sense of an earlier matter reaching its later result.
Yusuf promises to explain the prisoners’ dreams before their food arrives. The same root sense of تأويل is explicitly attached to a meaning that will be disclosed before a near future event.
After a period, the freed prisoner remembers Yusuf and offers to bring back the dreams’ تأويل. The verse stages delayed recall and interpretation; the king’s dream follows in verse 46.

The king’s dream is restated as seven fat cows, seven lean cows, and green and dry ears before Yusuf explains it. These crop images make the later storage plan in verses 47–49 answer a specific dream.
Yusuf’s father says God will choose him, teach him تأويل events, and complete His favor on Jacob’s family. The verse presents interpretation and favor as promised future outcomes.

After Yusuf is sold into Egypt, the verse says God establishes him there and teaches him interpretation of events. The later station and knowledge follow his earlier vulnerable one, as the section’s own-life reading allows.
The verse asks whether people await anything but the Quran’s تأويل; when it arrives, those who forgot it confess that the messengers brought truth. A delayed outcome reverses their earlier denial.
The deniers reject what they do not comprehend and whose تأويل has not yet come. This is a direct instance of the section’s outcome sense being unavailable before its time.
The command to return disputes to God and the Messenger is called خير and أحسن تأويلا. The verse joins the section’s “better” root to an explicit best outcome.

The verse pairs what has passed before and what comes after—ما تقدم من ذنبك وما تأخر—just before mentioning completion of favor. That is the section’s prior/later pair attached to a completed benefit.
The Hour makes their whole stay seem no more than an evening or its duha. The verse uses the exact morning-time word developed in the section as a measure for a life viewed from its end.

The verse tells the Prophet to be patient and not hasten punishment; when the promised event is seen, people seem to have stayed only an hour of a day. It joins waiting for what is promised to a compressed reckoning of the earlier time.
At the gathering, people think they stayed only an hour of a day before recognizing one another. Like 79:46, the end changes how the span before it is measured.
On the Hour, the criminals swear they stayed no more than an hour. Their short estimate makes the first life recede into a brief interval when its final scene arrives.
The believers answer the claim in verse 55: they remained until the Resurrection Day by God’s decree, though they did not know. This gives the apparent hour a longer, appointed span.
God asks how many years the people stayed on earth before the answer in verse 113. This sets up the section’s question of how a whole earlier life looks from its end.
They answer that they stayed a day or part of a day. The compressed duration parallels the life reduced to an evening or duha in 79:46.
God says they stayed only a little, had they known, then asks whether they thought they were created without purpose and would not return. The short first span is measured against return.
At the gathering, people whisper that they remained only ten days. It is another specific estimate of an earlier span as the final day arrives.
The most moderate of them says they remained only a day. This sharpens the previous estimate into the same end-time compression of life found in 79:46.
On the day God calls people, they answer praising Him and think they remained only a little. The call at the end changes the scale of the time before it.

A man is made to die for a hundred years and revived, yet estimates that he stayed a day or part of one. This makes elapsed time and the later return perceptibly different, as in the section’s end-time measure.
The verse asks whether the first creation wearied God, then says people are confused about a new creation. It explicitly connects the first beginning to a later creation.
The verse contrasts the known first creation with what follows and asks why people do not remember. It gives the section’s first/later ordering an explicit creation-and-return frame.
The verse says the second creation is upon God. This is the section’s named “second creation” sense of الدار الآخرة.
When asked who can revive decayed bones, the answer is the One who created them the first time. The first creation is made the ground for a later return.
The answer to doubt about resurrection is the One who created people the first time. This gives the section’s beginning/following relation a direct first-creation context.
The verse asks whether people see God begin creation and then repeat it. It states the first and later acts together, not merely a general afterlife theme.
God originates creation and repeats it; the return is easy for Him. This directly joins beginning to what follows.
The verse says God originates and repeats. Its concise pair matches the section’s ordering of first and later acts.
Moses is told that the staff will be returned to its former state, سيرتها الأولى, after appearing as a snake. The lexical “first” becomes a concrete before-and-after reversal.
The preceding surah states that the last and the first belong to God. It places the section’s exact pair under divine ownership.
The verse answers the disbelievers’ wishes by saying the Hereafter and the first life belong to God. It repeats the section’s two-abode pair in a distinct argumentative setting.
God is named the First and the Last, الأول والآخر. The shared pair preserves its temporal relation while applying it to God’s names.
The verse says praise belongs to God in the first life and the Hereafter, then says to Him is the return. It joins the section’s two time-periods to an explicit destination.
The verse states that the Hereafter is better and more lasting, matching the section’s explicit weighing of later against earlier.
The preceding verse says people prefer the nearer life. It supplies the opposing choice that makes the next verse’s better and more lasting Hereafter a reversal.
After noting differing ranks among people, the verse says the Hereafter is greater in degrees. It compares what comes later with distinctions in the present life.
Those who desire the immediate life are given some of it, then face Hell. This shows the limited near reward against the later reckoning.
Whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as a believer has effort appreciated. It presents the other choice from verse 18 and its later outcome.
The transgressor who prefers the worldly life is introduced before the statement that Hell is his home. It names the choice reversed by the section’s better-later measure.
The one who fears standing before the Lord and restrains desire is introduced before the Garden outcome. This is a specific stance toward the later life.
The Garden is said to be the home of the person described in verse 40. It completes the choice-and-outcome contrast.
The verse asks whether people are satisfied with worldly life over the Hereafter, then calls worldly enjoyment in the Hereafter little. It directly reverses the section’s valuation.
The verse describes those who prefer worldly life over the Hereafter and turn others from God’s path. It supplies a concrete contrary preference.
The verse describes one who turns away from remembrance and wants only worldly life. It marks the boundary of choosing the near life alone.
The verse says they bought worldly life at the price of the Hereafter. The purchase turns the section’s deferred-value image into a failed exchange.

What people have will perish, while what is with God remains; the patient are promised a better reward. This directly states the passing/remaining relation developed by the section’s later-time image.

After the garden’s collapse, the verse says true protection belongs to God and names the best reward and outcome, خيرا ثوابا وخير عقبا. This joins the section’s outcome sense of ء و ل to its better-later valuation.
The garden is described as vines surrounded by date palms, with cultivated land between them. This supplies the particular palm-and-crop scene that the following verse says bore fruit.

The owner imagines that, if returned to his Lord, he will find something better than the garden. His claim uses خيرا and an end or return, but mistakes present prosperity for a guaranteed better outcome.
The owner’s fruit is surrounded and the garden lies collapsed, leaving him to regret what he spent. The fruitful scene’s later destruction makes the end of a crop-bearing garden visible.

The verse pictures a garden of palms and vines destroyed by a fiery whirlwind when its owner is old and has young children. This is a direct reversal of the section’s palm retaining its yield to the end: waiting for the final crop can still end in loss.
The fruit is neither cut off nor forbidden. Its unending availability contrasts with the date palm’s finite last harvest and makes the lasting later reward concrete.

The verse says God brings out pasture before the following verse says it becomes dark debris; the same surah later says the Hereafter is better and more lasting. It stages the crop’s earlier flourishing against its later end.
The pasture becomes dark debris. This is the plant-life boundary between a season’s growth and its ending, near the surah’s explicit contrast of the near life with the lasting Hereafter.

The worldly life is compared to rain-fed growth that flourishes and then yellows and crumbles, before the verse contrasts punishment with forgiveness and approval in the Hereafter. It makes passing yield and final outcome one scene.
The oath is by the sun and its duha, ضحاها. The section’s dictionary entry for ض ح و names the bright time after sunrise, so the verse shares its precise sunlit interval.
God makes night dark and brings out its duha, ضحاها. It directly locates the morning brightness named in the section against the preceding night.

The verse says only God knows the تأويل of the ambiguous verses. This may mean their ultimate reality rather than the section’s outcome sense, but it specifically marks interpretation as knowledge whose final reach is not presently available.
The prisoners ask Yusuf to explain their visions, using تأويل. Their dreams receive particular outcomes later, making this a concrete use of the section’s result/interpretation sense.

Moses sees a wall about to collapse, which Khidr repairs without taking a fee; verse 82 later explains the protected treasure beneath it. The scene sets up provision preserved for the orphans’ future.
Just measure is called better and أحسن تأويلا. The verse gives the section’s “outcome” sense a concrete ethical case: fair dealing leads to the better end.

One who seeks the harvest of the Hereafter has it increased, while one who seeks the world receives some of it without a share in the next life. It makes the two temporal destinations into distinct harvests.
The verse says the Hereafter’s home is better for those mindful of God than worldly play and diversion. It develops the same comparative value of the later abode.
When the mindful are asked what God sent down, they answer “good,” and the verse says the Hereafter’s home is better. It repeats the section’s ranking in a question-and-answer setting.
Worldly enjoyment is contrasted with what is with God, which is better and more lasting. It makes the section’s later benefit explicitly endure.
Wealth and children adorn worldly life, while lasting good deeds are better for reward and hope. The verse contrasts temporary present goods with what lasts.
What people receive is called worldly enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more lasting for believers. It states the passing/remaining distinction alongside the section’s later valuation.
The verse calls worldly life play and amusement and says the Hereafter’s home is the true life. It makes the later state the enduring reality.
The verse calls this world a temporary enjoyment and the Hereafter the home of settlement. It directly contrasts the temporary first span with what follows.
The verse warns against coveting worldly adornment and calls the Lord’s provision better and more lasting. It connects the section’s future gift to enduring provision.
The supplication asks for good in this world and good in the Hereafter. It frames the two lives as distinct matters for which the worshipper asks what is good, echoing the section’s istikhara gloss.
The verse says God creates and chooses, while people have no choice, الخيرة. The section’s خ ي ر branch includes choosing between things; this verse marks the boundary of who chooses.

The verse explicitly gives the alternatives of belief and disbelief to whoever wills, then states the fire’s consequence. The section’s خ ي ر dictionary branch includes leaving someone a choice between two matters; here the choice has a defined boundary.
The two gardens yield their produce without loss, with a river between them. It makes the fruit-bearing garden in verse 32 a scene of provision before the later boast and ruin.
Entering his garden, the owner says he does not think it will ever perish or that the Hour will come. His confidence in permanence is reversed when the garden is ruined in verse 42.

The companion hopes his Lord will give him a garden better than the owner’s and send a calamity on the present one. It gives a concrete contrast between current yield and a hoped-for later replacement.
The Garden of the Hereafter has abundant fruit. This connects fruit-bearing to the later life named in the section, though this verse by itself does not describe a harvest time.
The good tree gives its fruit at every season by its Lord’s permission. It is a specific recurring yield that helps a reader see the temporal pattern behind the section’s retained fruit.
Worldly life is likened to rain-fed plants that flourish, then become harvestable and turn to debris. Its growth-to-ending sequence gives a crop image for the section’s weighing of what comes later.
Worldly life is like rain that grows plants before they dry and scatter as fragments. The verse makes a plant’s temporary yield a concrete contrast to the enduring good deeds named next.

The verse follows rain through plants of different colors until they yellow and become debris. It supplies a specific growth-to-end cycle like the section’s crop image, while leaving its afterlife comparison unstated here.
The oath names night as it covers. Beside the next verse’s day appearing, it gives a dark-to-light sequence that helps place the section’s dawn threshold within a day.
The oath names day as it appears, والنهار إذا تجلى. This is the increase of daylight that corresponds to the section’s stages after sunrise.
The appointment for the gathering is the Day of Adornment, with people gathered at duha. It gives the section’s named morning interval a specific appointed time.

The verse asks whether people feel secure from punishment arriving at duha while they play. The morning scene is a normal threshold before a later reckoning, adding a specific reversal to the section’s unfinished, bright day.
The verse says God brings the truth and the best تأويلا in answer to the opponents’ arguments. It uses the section’s named interpretation root for a later, decisive explanation.
The king’s interpreters call the dreams confused and say they do not know their تأويل. Their failed present reading contrasts with Yusuf’s later, specific account.
The king’s dream joins fat and lean cows to green and dry ears; the next verses ask Yusuf for its interpretation and forecast stored grain. It introduces the crop-and-later-provision sequence.

The sleepers estimate that they stayed a day or part of one, unaware of the long span before waking. This is a parallel in perceived duration to 79:46, though it concerns sleep rather than the Hereafter.

The garden owners swear to cut their crop in the morning, expecting a later yield from what they have kept growing. This is a direct harvest-time scene against the section’s palm whose fruit remains until the final picking.
While they sleep, an affliction from their Lord passes over the garden overnight. The verse supplies the intervening delay that turns the planned morning harvest into a lost one.
The garden is found as though cut down or blackened. This reverses the section’s image of fruit remaining on the tree through the harvest season.
The owners call one another at daybreak. This is the morning threshold at which the planned harvest is to begin.
They urge one another to go early to their crop if they mean to reap it. The verse makes the harvest timing explicit.
They reach the garden early, determined to keep the poor from it. This continues the planned harvest and shows that its expected yield is already treated as secured.
When they see the garden, they think they have lost their way. Their first expectation of a harvest is reversed by the ruined crop.
They realize instead that they have been deprived. This names the outcome of a crop they expected to gather later.
After the garden is lost, its owners hope their Lord will replace it with something better, خيرا منها. The verse gives the section’s خ ي ر sense a concrete later compensation after an earlier loss.
The verse says the punishment of the Hereafter is greater than this punishment. It sets the garden’s present loss beside a later consequence.

The verse pictures tall date palms with clustered fruit. It gives the section’s dictionary image of a palm carrying its crop a concrete Quranic scene; the previous and following verses supply rain and provision.
The verse calls the produce provision for servants and says dead land is revived by it, “thus the emergence.” Its own contribution connects yielded provision to the later return.
God says He has decreed death among people and cannot be outdone. This makes the first life’s endpoint appointed, alongside the section’s later creation and outcome.
The following verse says God can change people’s forms and bring them into an unknown form. It completes the preceding decree of death with the later transformation.
All on earth is described as perishing. This marks the finite end of the first, earthly span against what remains.
The face of the Lord, possessor of majesty and honor, is said to remain. It supplies the enduring side of the perishing/remaining boundary.
Those before are made to taste disgrace in worldly life, while the punishment of the Hereafter is greater. The later outcome outweighs the earlier one in the opposite, punitive direction.

Those who emigrated after being wronged are promised a good place in this world, while the reward of the Hereafter is greater. It is a specific present/later valuation tied to a real change of circumstance.
People love the immediate life and leave behind a heavy day. This is an explicit preference for the near term over the later one, contrary to the section’s valuation.
The verse says people love the immediate life. It isolates the first side of the contrast completed by the next verse.
The verse says they leave the Hereafter. Together with verse 20, it names the contrary choice to the section’s better-later weighing.
At the end, a person regrets not having sent deeds ahead for “my life.” The verse makes the earlier opportunity and later reckoning one concrete sequence.

The verse asks who seeks the reward of this world, then says with God is the reward of both this world and the Hereafter. It places both temporal rewards under one owner, as in the section’s first/last pair.

The verse says each soul dies only by God’s permission at a written term, then distinguishes those seeking the world’s reward from those seeking the Hereafter’s. It joins appointed timing to a choice between the two rewards.
After the believers’ prayer, God gives them the reward of this world and the best reward of the Hereafter. This is a concrete instance of a later reward completing an earlier trial.

The verse asks whether it should tell the God-fearing of something better than worldly desires, then names gardens and God’s pleasure. It turns the section’s choice of the better of two matters into a direct world/Hereafter comparison.

The verse says people may dislike something that is good for them and love something that is bad, while God knows and they do not. It supplies a specific reversal in how an outcome is judged, related to the section’s better choice.

The captives are told that if God knows good in their hearts, He will give them better than what was taken from them and forgive them. This is a concrete later compensation for an earlier taking, using the section’s better-choice root.

After Yusuf’s story of reversal and establishment, the verse says the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and fear God. It is another explicit statement of the section’s later-abode valuation.

The preceding surah ends by promising that the one who gives seeking his Lord’s face will surely be satisfied, ولَسَوْفَ يَرْضَىٰ. This closely matches the section’s affirmed future gift ending in satisfaction.
The verse says that with hardship comes ease. It offers a specific before/after parallel to the section’s comparison of the later state with the earlier one.
The repeated assurance says again that with hardship comes ease. Its repetition makes the later relief certain, like the section’s emphatic promise of what is to come.
The oath names the morning as it brightens. This is a precise light-increasing threshold parallel to the section’s post-sunrise sequence.
The verse says the warning is for whoever wishes to advance or lag behind. This directly names the section’s first/later relation as movement forward or backward, with the warning as its boundary.
Every soul is then said to be held in pledge for what it earned. This supplies the later accounting that follows the advance/lag choice in verse 37.
The oath names the night as it departs. This gives the dark side of the transition completed by the next verse’s breathing morning.
The oath names the morning as it breathes. That image matches the section’s light increasing at a threshold after sunrise.
Each community has an appointed term, and when it comes it cannot be delayed or advanced. This is a direct statement of a fixed endpoint for the section’s deferred-time image.
Each community has a term; when it arrives, it cannot be delayed or advanced even an hour. The verse repeats the section’s fixed-endpoint relation with an explicit measure of time.
No community precedes its term or delays it. This states the boundary around postponement in the section’s timed promise.
The people are called to worship and forgiveness, and God will defer them to a specified term; once it comes, it cannot be delayed. It joins a promised respite to its fixed end.
The call to seek forgiveness is followed by a promise of good enjoyment until an appointed term and a reward for every possessor of bounty. This is provision granted over a bounded future interval.
The punishment is delayed until a countable term, and the deniers ask what is holding it back. The verse makes postponement itself a challenge before the promised outcome.
The messengers say God calls people to seek forgiveness and will defer them to an appointed term. It is a direct instance of respite with a later deadline.
God does not overlook wrongdoers; He only postpones them to a day when eyes stare. The verse makes the deferred reckoning explicit.

People ask for punishment to be hastened, but God will not fail His promise; a day with Him is like a thousand years by their count. It links delay to a radically different measure of the promised time.
The verse says that if God hastened evil for people as they hasten good, their term would already have been concluded. It makes the contrast between human haste and deferred divine timing explicit.
The deniers are warned not to mistake their reprieve for good; the respite increases their burden before humiliating punishment. This is a boundary on reading delay as a guaranteed benefit.
God is said to create people from clay and then set a term, with another specified term known to Him. This ties the beginning of human life to its appointed later limit.

God promises many gains, hastens one for the believers, and holds another gain they could not yet reach within His power. It is a specific promised benefit divided between an immediate portion and a later one.

God confirms the Messenger’s earlier vision and promises entry into the Sacred Mosque, with a near victory placed before it. The verse joins an earlier sign to its later fulfillment for the same addressee.
Yusuf welcomes his parents and family into Egypt in safety just before naming the fulfillment of his former dream. This is the reunion that precedes the delayed dream’s completion in verse 100.
Moses says his Lord knows who will have the good outcome of the Home. This uses the section’s endpoint/result idea to frame the final outcome beyond a present dispute.
